'''Charles Jeffrey Brinker''' (known as '''C. Jeffrey Brinker''') is an American materials scientist and engineer. He is a Distinguished and Regents' Professor Emeritus at the [[University of New Mexico]] (UNM) and a Sandia Fellow Emeritus at [[Sandia National Laboratories]]. Brinker is best known for his pioneering research in [[sol-gel processing]], molecular self-assembly, porous and nanostructured materials, and the development of mesoporous silica–lipid hybrid nanoparticles known as ''protocells'' for targeted drug delivery. He is a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]], the [[National Academy of Inventors]], and the [[National Academy of Sciences]], and a [[Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].

== Early life and education ==
Brinker was born in [[Easton, Pennsylvania]]. He attended [[Rutgers University]], where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree with high honors in 1972, a Master of Science degree in 1975, and a Ph.D. in 1978, all in Ceramic Science and Engineering.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Case to Increase the Support of Doctoral Students Across the New Brunswick-Piscataway Campus of Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey |url=https://oirap.rutgers.edu/msa/Documents/SupportCase-fulldoc.pdf |publisher=Rutgers University}}</ref>

== Career ==

Brinker began his professional career at [[Sandia National Laboratories]] in 1979 as a member of the technical staff, later serving as a Distinguished Member of the Technical Staff until 1998.<ref>{{cite web |title=Get to Know ACS Nano's C. Jeffrey Brinker |url=https://axial.acs.org/nanoscience/c-jeffrey-brinker |website=ACS Publications Chemistry|date=19 March 2020}}</ref> In 1991, Brinker also began a joint academic appointment at the [[University of New Mexico]] (UNM) as Distinguished National Laboratory Professor of Chemistry and Chemical and Nuclear Engineering, serving in this role until 1999. In 1999, he was appointed Professor of Chemistry and Chemical and Nuclear Engineering at UNM, a position he held until 2006.<ref name=unm>{{cite web |title=Jeffrey Brinker |url=https://cbe.unm.edu/faculty-staff/faculty-profiles/jeffrey-brinker.html |website=The University of New Mexico}}</ref>

From 1999 to 2003, Brinker concurrently served as a Senior Scientist in the Chemical Synthesis and Nanomaterials Department at Sandia National Laboratories. In 2003, he was named a Laboratory Fellow at Sandia<ref>{{cite web |title=Jeff Brinker, Jim Gosler appointed Sandia Fellows |url=https://www.sandia.gov/labnews/2003/09/19/key09-19-03-storiesfellows/ |website=LabNews}}</ref> and served in that role until 2019.

At UNM, Brinker was appointed Regents’ Professor of Chemical and Nuclear Engineering and Molecular Genetics and Microbiology in 2006 and designated Distinguished Professor in 2008. In 2010, he became a member of the UNM Comprehensive Cancer Center.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bio :: Brinker Group: Nanostructures Research |url=https://brinkerlab.unm.edu/c.j-brinker/index.html |website=University of New Mexico}}</ref> From 2006 to 2020, he also served as a Distinguished Affiliate Scientist at the Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies, a U.S. Department of Energy research center.<ref name=unm /> Since 2020, he has served as an associate editor of ''[[ACS Nano]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=ACS Nano Editorial Board – ACS Publications |url=https://pubs.acs.org/page/ancac3/editors.html |website=ACS |access-date=18 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Following his retirement from full-time academic duties, he was named Distinguished and Regents’ Professor Emeritus at UNM.<ref name=unm />

== Research ==
Brinker’s research spans [[sol–gel]] chemistry, porous and nanostructured materials, organic–inorganic hybrid materials, and nano–bio interfaces. A recurring theme of his work has been the investigation of relationships between synthesis methods, material structure, and resulting physical and chemical properties in solution-derived inorganic systems. His work has also explored biomimetic approaches to materials design, in which structural features observed in natural systems are replicated using inorganic materials.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sellinger |first1=A. |last2=Weiss |first2=P. M. |last3=Nguyen |first3=A. |last4=Lu |first4=Y. |last5=Assink |first5=R. A. |last6=Gong |first6=W. |last7=Brinker |first7=C. J. |title=Continuous self-assembly of organic–inorganic nanocomposite coatings that mimic nacre |journal=Nature |year=1998 |volume=394 |issue=6690 |pages=256–260 |doi=10.1038/28354}}</ref>

In parallel with his research activities, Brinker played a role in promoting interdisciplinary approaches within materials science, including through his involvement with the [[Materials Research Society]] symposium series ''Better Ceramics Through Chemistry'', which ran through multiple editions during the 1980s and 1990s and later evolved into symposium series on organic–inorganic hybrid materials.<ref>See ''Better Ceramics Through Chemistry I–VI'', Materials Research Society Symposium Proceedings (1984–1994).</ref>

He co-authored the textbook ''Sol-Gel Science: The Physics and Chemistry of Sol-Gel Processing'' (1990), which describes the physical and chemical principles underlying sol–gel processing and has been widely cited in the materials science literature.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bhaduri |first1=S. B. |title=The Physics and Chemistry of Sol-Gel Processing edited by C. J. Brinker and G. W. Scherer |journal=Materials and Manufacturing Processes |date=1 May 1993 |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=391–392 |doi=10.1080/10426919308934843}}</ref> His early research examined mechanisms of [[hydrolysis]], [[condensation (chemistry)|condensation]], [[gelation]], and [[sintering]] in [[silicate]] systems, contributing to the development of [[glass]]es, [[thin film]] coatings, and particulate materials processed under relatively mild conditions.

During the 1990s, Brinker and collaborators developed an ambient-pressure drying method for silica [[aerogel]]s, addressing limitations associated with [[supercritical drying]]. The approach involved surface modification of wet gels to reduce condensation reactions and capillary stresses during drying, allowing the material to recover porosity after shrinkage. This work demonstrated a pathway toward lower-cost aerogel production and influenced subsequent commercial manufacturing methods.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Prakash |first1=S. S. |last2=Brinker |first2=C. J. |last3=Hurd |first3=A. J. |last4=Rao |first4=S. M. |title=Silica aerogel films prepared at ambient pressure by using surface derivatization to induce reversible drying shrinkage |journal=Nature |year=1995 |volume=374 |issue=6521 |pages=439–443 |doi=10.1038/374439a0}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=When love-hate is materially good |url=https://www.snexplores.org/article/when-love-hate-materially-good |publisher=Science News Explores |date=13 October 2010}}</ref>

In the late 1990s, Brinker and collaborators introduced evaporation-induced self-assembly (EISA), a processing strategy in which solvent evaporation promotes the organization of [[surfactant]]–inorganic composites into ordered [[mesoporous material]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brinker |first1=C. J. |last2=Lu |first2=Y. |last3=Sellinger |first3=A. |last4=Fan |first4=H. |title=Evaporation-Induced Self-Assembly: Nanostructures Made Easy |journal=Advanced Materials |year=1999 |volume=11 |issue=7 |pages=579–585 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1521-4095(199905)11:7<579::AID-ADMA579>3.0.CO;2-R}}</ref> The method enabled the fabrication of mesoporous silica as uniform thin films via [[dip coating]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Y. |last2=Ganguli |first2=R. |last3=Drewien |first3=C. A. |last4=Anderson |first4=M. T. |last5=Brinker |first5=C. J. |title=Continuous formation of supported cubic and hexagonal mesoporous films by sol–gel dip-coating |journal=Nature |year=1997 |volume=389 |issue=6649 |pages=364–368 |doi=10.1038/38699}}</ref> and was later extended to the formation of spherical mesoporous nanoparticles using aerosol-assisted processing.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Y. |last2=Fan |first2=H. |last3=Stump |first3=A. |last4=Ward |first4=T. L. |last5=Rieker |first5=T. |last6=Brinker |first6=C. J. |title=Aerosol-assisted self-assembly of mesostructured spherical nanoparticles |journal=Nature |year=1999 |volume=398 |issue=6724 |pages=223–226 |doi=10.1038/18410}}</ref>

Subsequent studies expanded EISA-based approaches to include organic–inorganic nanocomposites,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sellinger |first1=A. |last2=Weiss |first2=P. M. |last3=Nguyen |first3=A. |last4=Lu |first4=Y. |last5=Assink |first5=R. A. |last6=Gong |first6=W. |last7=Brinker |first7=C. J. |title=Continuous self-assembly of organic–inorganic nanocomposite coatings that mimic nacre |journal=Nature |year=1998 |volume=394 |pages=256–260 |doi=10.1038/28354}}</ref> ordered nanoparticle–silica arrays,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=H. |last2=Yang |first2=K. |last3=Boye |first3=D. M. |last4=Sigmon |first4=T. |last5=Malloy |first5=K. J. |last6=Xu |first6=H. |last7=López |first7=G. P. |last8=Brinker |first8=C. J. |title=Self-assembly of ordered, robust, three-dimensional gold nanocrystal/silica arrays |journal=Science |year=2004 |volume=304 |issue=5670 |pages=567–571 |doi=10.1126/science.1095140}}</ref> optically responsive nanopores, and low-dielectric mesoporous films. EISA-based methods have since been applied in the fabrication of membranes, sensors, low-dielectric materials, and nanocomposites across materials science and [[nanotechnology]].<ref>{{cite web |title=WHAT'S NEXT; Molecules Engineered With an Inkjet Printer |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/05/25/technology/what-s-next-molecules-engineered-with-an-inkjet-printer.html |publisher=The New York Times |date=25 May 2000}}</ref>

From the late 2000s onward, Brinker’s research increasingly addressed nano–bio interfaces and applications in [[nanomedicine]]. This work included the development of mesoporous silica nanoparticles encapsulated by supported [[lipid bilayer]]s, commonly referred to as ''protocells'', designed for the delivery of therapeutic and diagnostic cargos. Such systems have been investigated for applications in [[cancer therapy]], [[vaccine]] delivery, and [[biosensor]] development.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashley |first1=C. E. |last2=Carnes |first2=E. C. |last3=Phillips |first3=G. K. |last4=Durfee |first4=P. N. |last5=Buley |first5=M. D. |last6=Loo |first6=C. |last7=Brinker |first7=C. J. |title=The targeted delivery of multicomponent cargos to cancer cells by nanoporous particle-supported lipid bilayers |journal=Nature Materials |year=2011 |volume=10 |issue=5 |pages=389–397 |doi=10.1038/nmat2992|pmc=3287066 }}</ref>
